utterances.text: Period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, again the letter has been authenticated by this witness. I think the date, obviously, the translation is what was written, but obviously the location and the timing clearly would give an indication that the '92 should be '94. Other than that, we think that it obviously is relevant. This witness has denied receiving it. However, the contents of the letter themselves are relevant to the issue of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is certainly relevant for impeachment purposes. The request is whether you have laid the proper foundation. That is the problem. The witness identifies the handwriting, but she has never received the letter. So, I guess you are offering it as an admission of some sort, but what? You tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point we would mark it as 354 for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We will simply proffer it again through another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Very good. I thought you were trying to get it in now. Fine. It has been marked for identification purposes. The witness has identified the handwriting and we will move on to another topic or are you going to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated, Mrs. Tadic, that you went to work in Libya in 1986 and returned in late 1986, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that Dusko Tadic had followed you later in 1986. When did he arrive in Libya?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere in mid summer, June/July. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When did you all return in late 86, what month, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not return together. I returned first and he returned a month after I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: OK. When did you return and when did he return, the months, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned on 25th November 1996 and he returned around 20th December 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said prior to him going to Libya he had a karate school -- yes, I am sorry. Your answer was translated as "1996". I believe you meant to say "1986", is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: '86, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic also go to classes or teach classes in the town of Prijedor itself at the Mladost sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that when he returned from Libya he did not get involved in the karate school in Kozarac again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he still partly own that school or had it all been turned over to Emir Karabasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, officially he was registered as the coach of that school, but when he went to Libya the trainings were not carried out regularly, so basically it died out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said when you were building your cafe in Kozarac that you received a lot of help from your neighbours in Kozarac and that the building of the cafe was financed through a combination of money from Dusko Tadic's brother and by loans from neighbours. Those were, in fact, some substantial loans from Muslim neighbours, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Answer, please, Mrs. Tadic. Is that "yes" or "no"? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that you and your husband joined the SDS together and that it was in part because of the threatening letter that you had received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that you had received no political books or documents regarding the philosophy or the policies of the SDS before or after joining it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think they had any books.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Well, then in what way did you think that joining the SDS was going to assist you, if you did not know what it stood for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew the programme of the SDS, and it was enough for us to know that that Party wanted us to stay in Yugoslavia which was our homeland, and that was enough for us in order to join it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why do you think that the SDS wanted Serbs to stay in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they wanted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that your husband was picked to run the plebiscite and you were picked as one of the delegates because you had free time. Were you not at that time working at the hospital in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I said that we had free time and my husband had free time -- my husband had free time and I helped him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was not your husband busy running the cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the head of the cafe and he had people who worked for him, employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also had two young daughters at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was already a bit older and the other one was small. Both of them were not small.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So the other Serbs that lived in Kozarac had more obligations than you two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the others were older; they were not as young as we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The plebiscite had different coloured ballots for Serbs and for non-Serbs, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Some non-Serbs did vote in the plebiscite, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but why would the ballots be of a different colour? I do not understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You do not recall that the ballots were of a different colour and had different phrasing on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that you read the Islamic declaration by Alija Izetbegovic. What did you see as the main thesis or premise of that work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand. Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you read the book, what did you take away as the main premise, the main thesis, of the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to my mind, the most important thesis of the book was to wait, that the Muslim obtain 53 per cent so they would be more numerous, that is, take power and all the people that lived there should live under Islamic laws. I am not really a politician. I cannot know how to explain it to you well. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before they bring the witness in, I would like to have a brief session regarding that letter, if we could?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. That has been marked for identification purposes as 354 for the record. OK. Go ahead, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will begin while I am waiting for Miss Sutherland to bring some copies -- here she is.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: More copies of the letter -- you are optimistic!

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in terms of clarifying this issue about the letter, if I could have three copies for the Bench and one copy for the Defence? What I am handing up to the Court, your Honour, and to the Defence are a series of motions which were filed and then withdrawn by the Defence, the first beginning on 23rd June.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do we want to make this an Exhibit or are they a part of the record? They are a part of our record. No -- yes, they are. Tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We would like to make them a part of the record, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Tell me what they are and then we will decide whether we need to make them an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, the first one beginning on 3rd July 1995, a motion to suppress the production of evidence obtained from the accused. On page 3 of that motion, paragraphs 11 through 14, the Defence refers to, "While in detention in Germany, the accused has written private letters. Those letters were then confiscated, copied" ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Wait, let me follow you, 11 through 14? This motion, I think, if I remember, was withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It was, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It has been a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. My point in raising it is that as of 3rd July 1995, the Defence were certainly aware of the letters. In fact, they were making a motion to prevent their production into evidence. That motion was followed up by a second motion to suppress on 4th September 1995, again referring to the letters. On 28th September 1995 there was a notice of withdrawal of these motions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Help us, we have received so many. Tell us, do you want us to start from the bottom up or the top down?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I think the way they are organised, it is bottom up, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. The first thing then we have is a request for an extension of the date to file a motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Of course, yes, 3rd July 1995 is the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: 23rd June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: 23rd June, yes, your Honour. I am sorry, that is right. That was just the request. The actual motion was then filed on 3rd July 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We responded on 28th July (which we did not provide to you since it is not relevant to the issue at this point) to this particular issue. Then the Defence filed the second motion on 4th September 1995 again which we replied to. Both of those motions referred to these letters from the prison. The next document is 28th September 1995, the notice of withdrawal. Then in response to a fax letter which I sent, the last document is a response from Mr. Wladimiroff to my attention. In paragraph 2 you will see that, in fact, the Defence does no longer maintain the position that the German material is inadmissible evidence for the reasons stated in the motions. However, they did reserve the right to raise additional objections. So, in point of fact, just for the point of clarification, we certainly had a reasonable grounds for believing that the Defence was not only aware but had copies of these letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The letter is mentioned by date in some of these motions, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I do not believe it is, your Honour, no. They simply refer to letters "confiscated" and "copied" at the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think it also says letters seized by the German authorities, but if I heard Mr. Wladimiroff correctly and if I understand your position, these were - this letter, 354, was in the material submitted by the German lawyer. Was it in the ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: There is -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- folder from the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: There are really two separate seized documents or categories, if you will. These particular letters, and as they are referred to here in the motion, were letters that were taken and copied by the German authorities while he was in prison. These materials are separate from those which were seized from the house in Munich where he was arrested. These letters which we received were in binder No. 4 of the German materials, as I referred to before. The Defence received binders, we received our copy of binders 1 through 10 from the German authorities. The Defence received their copies of binders 1 through 10 from the Defence counsel in Germany who had been given his copy by the German authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: He simply turned over his materials to the Defence here. We then showed them the additional four binders which we had, binders 11 to 14, the seized documents, essentially.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Was the letter included in what you showed the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the letter was included in binder No. 4. We had no reason to believe that, as they maintain, their copy does not have these letters. They never at any time asked us for a copy of these letters, despite the fact that they obviously referred to them in their motion in 3rd July 1995, which is why we believed they had copies.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The problem, of course, is that it just talks about "letters". Then the other problem is, I do not know how I can determine whether this particular letter was in the binder received by Mr. Wladimiroff. He says it was not, and you say it was included in the binder that you received and that you also showed them the binder that you received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The only reason we are raising this again is for a matter of clarification as to why we believed they had possession of those materials, since they referred to them in a motion specifically. There were only a certain number of letters from the prison. They never asked us for copies additionally, and so we will certainly rectify that situation. We would invite them to review their binder 4 very thoroughly, though, to make sure that it is not there before we do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Perhaps, only as a matter of curiosity, but this was a letter written after, of course, the accused's arrest?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: How would it have ever been discovered -- the searches were at the time of his arrest, I take it, were they, and it would not be in existence at that time, and it was a letter from him to his wife, how did it ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This was a letter written while he was in prison ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: --- and under the German rules of detention, any outgoing mail is subject to seizure ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: --- review and photocopying. That was provided to the accused. He knew that. That was in the regulations. It was all part of the documents which is why the Defence withdrew the motion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But Mr. Wladimiroff says this letter was not among what he received, I think. Is that correct, Mr. Wladimiroff? Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, your Honour, in the motion itself no letter is specified, just as an issue as such ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- it was raised. You may have seen that I made a reservation when I withdrew, saying that the withdrawal does not, of course, mean that the probative value of this evidence may not be criticised by the Defence. Here we are. As a matter of fact, the witness told you that she did not receive the letter. So, apparently, it was seized by the German authorities. There was no disclosure by the Prosecution to us. They assumed that we got the letter. It was not established as a fact. As I said, it was not specified in our motion. But maybe there is a lot of fuss about nothing because we have been reading the letter in the meantime. We feel the letter is very exculpatory, so we would even like to have it produced.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, all of this back and forth, you have no objection to the letter, is that what you are now telling me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour. Having had an opportunity to read it, we view it as exculpatory. The difficulty here is introducing it to this witness. It seems, from what the Prosecution are telling us, that it was seized by the German authorities as a communication at some stage whilst the defendant was in custody and, of course, she says she has never seen it. I do not know if it was seized, copied and then went back into the post or whether it was just seized, period.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There are two issues, one, just as to whether or not you had ever seen it. So that is really just an issue of surprise. As I said earlier, I do not know how I can resolve it unless I were to sit with you, you know, when you receive these folders and determine what was in your folder and what was in the folder of the Prosecutor. That is one issue just in terms of the surprise. The other has to do with the admissibility. What Mr. Wladimiroff has said is that he reserved the right to raise any claim as to probative value. That I do not know really deals with the question of admissibility. In other words, what he is saying, it is relevant, it may be admissible, but it is not really probative of the facts. But then the third issue, I guess, is whether it is admissible through this witness. If you have no objection, do you still wish to offer 354, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have no objection to 354, but it is a question of how it is dealt with in evidence, because this witness has said that she has never seen it and, as it is written by someone's else, it then becomes impossible for her to deal with it if it is not something that she has acted upon or seen or had any views upon at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you have no objection to its admissibility, but you, I gather, have some concern about whether this will be used to question this witness ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- and you consider that would be inappropriate since she has not received it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I have already indicated my questions for the letter with this witness were done before it was even resolved, so no. But, as to the issue, since obviously the Defence knew there were letters since they described what was in them and these binders are sequentially numbered, the documents, so it should be fairly easy for them to determine if there is a document missing, a document missing in these binders. We would invite them to look carefully since there were other letters that might be proffered later on.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exactly. That is the question I have. We are beyond this issue, this is admissible because there is no objection, but no questioning of this witness. I am really concerned as to whether this is going to arise again. I am sure that we have no desire -- do you have any desire to sit with counsel and compare what is in your folder with what is in your folder, but we will do it, if necessary, in order to avoid a future problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it would be easier if the Prosecution are going to produce them in evidence to give us the copies that they intend to produce so that we can look at them overnight and review any to see if we have any objection to their admissibility. It seems to me that that would be a proper way and it is obviously a matter easily achieved.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You do not have the folders with you that you received?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have the folders, but we have never had an index from the Prosecution of material that they have; it was always left on the basis that, "Well, you have been served that by your German lawyer and that is good enough for you". But whether the German lawyers gave us an entire bundle, we do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Maybe you can sit with each other when we finish at 5.30 and make sure that the Defence has everything that is in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I indicated before, I am a little concerned about how this is being categorised. This information was given to them a long time ago. Each page, each document, is sequentially numbered. It is very easy to determine if you are missing a document in all of the binders. They simply need to go through them and say, "We do not have these numbers" and then we will provide those. But it seems to me that they were clearly referred to, not only in where they came from, that is, detention in Germany, but the content.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, but I gather there are not so many letters that you cannot sit down together at 5.30 and make sure that the Defence has what you think that they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We can give them a list of the dates of the letters, certainly, your Honour. We can certainly do that, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can that be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It can be done. I presume that these letters are in Serbo-Croat. If the Prosecution have translations that they can produce to us now, that will save us sending everything out to be translated in anticipation that some of the letters might be used. I think it would be much easier if they just gave us the letters that they intend to use in cross-examination so that we can have them with the translations.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Get together, please, at 5.30. Make sure that the two files are the same. If you have any translations, is there any problem with giving the translations ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Of course not, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- to the Defence at this time? OK. Will you do that? Sit down, compare your files and make sure you are talking about the same information. Then we will not have to worry about it, at least on that issue in terms of receipt. There may be other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am grateful to your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Very good. Is there anything else before Mrs. Tadic is brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good. 354 is admitted. Mrs. Tadic, please, should come in. MRS. MIRA TADIC, recalled. Cross-examined by MR. KEEGAN, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, did you offer the Serbo-Croatian as well as the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I would like to have them A and B, as is the usual custom.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. 354A will be the Serbo-Croatian translation, 354B the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, would you continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, you referred to the threatening letter which you received in 1990. There was, in fact, an investigation done with respect to that letter by the police, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was supposed to be done. It was supposed to be done.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Sorry, we did not get anything. We are not hearing you either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Supposedly it should have been done.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am hearing. Can you hear me, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I can now, I think my channel had been changed. (To the witness): In fact, the investigation was done and is it not true that there was no determination that that letter had been sent by Muslims in Kozarac? But, in fact, did not the investigation in its later stages begin focusing on the fact that perhaps you and your husband had fabricated that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the investigation was not based on that but on the Muslims from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that there was some change in the relationship between your husband and Emir Karabasic in 1991. What was the nature of that change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not see each other as frequently as they used to previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of circumstances caused that change, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the formation of national parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This was after the time that you and your husband had joined the SDS, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, previously. All the other parties along ethnic lines were formed prior to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: My question was the change in the relationship between Dusko Tadic and Emir Karabasic occurred after you and your ex-husband joined the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it has nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You described that there was during this same time, 1991, the change in the circumstances or the environment in the town of Kozarac, that the cafe was boycotted by Muslims from the centre of Kozarac and that there were rumours about the cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were not these people, the Muslims from the centre of Kozarac and throughout the area, the same people who had been your friends and your ex-husband's friends for all of your lives, the same people who had lent you a significant amount of money just a year prior so that you could build your cafe, and did you not, in fact, still employ Muslims as waiters in your cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we still employed Muslims as waiters in our cafe and we continued to socialise with some Muslims from Kozarac, but not with all of them as -- until that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So prior to this period of time had you socialised with all of the Muslims in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During this same time, was there not a significant build-up in the number of Serbian troops who were returning from the war in Croatia and being established in positions particularly in the hills around the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a stepping up in the number of troops but they were not positioned in town, but in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So the troop formations were only in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because I watched lorries drive by to Mrakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You watched them drive by the cafe, up the road to Mrakovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, going to work and coming home from work, I would encounter lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You stated that your overall goal was to continue to run the cafe and to live in Kozarac to raise your children there. If that was your goal, why did you not think of joining the SDA whose stated platform was for democracy and a multi-cultural Bosnia or even the HDZ? Why did you join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the SDS because their platform was to stay within Yugoslavia and protect the Serb people; whereas SDA had a platform which appealed only to Muslims and there was no democracy in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Despite the number of extremists in Kozarac, Muslim extremists, as you described them, and the number of armed people, in fact, the Orthodox church in Kozarac and the house of the priest which is on the property were never destroyed or, in fact, harmed in any way, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that when you were leaving Kozarac you recognised Sead Bahonjic as the man at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What kind of glasses was he wearing? Were they sunglasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was he also ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dark sunglasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: --- wearing a cap, a beret of some type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did he say when you told him that you were going to be back to the police station to get authorisation to leave Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. He said we could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The house that you lived in in Banja Luka, the one that you pointed out in the pictures today here in Court, to whom did you pay rent for that apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not paying rent in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You described that you arrived in Banja Luka on the Sunday evening and you started getting that apartment ready, you stayed with Ljubo and then started getting that apartment ready the very next day on the Monday, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did not start preparing things on the day after. We found the apartment in the evening on the day after, and then as of Tuesday we started to get it ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You stated that you and your ex-husband only had a personal automobile during a short period of time in your marriage in the early 80s, I guess, or mid 80s, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around the time between '80/'81 until '85, we sold it before we went to Libya.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During those years before the war and up until the time of the war, though, many of your Muslim neighbours in Kozarac had personal vehicles, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Including Volkswagen Golfs and even Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You referred to the people that you knew in Banja Luka as "real friends". What does that mean? What kind of friends are those, "real friends"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means people we always saw and visited whenever we went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How were those different from the friends that you saw and visited in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no difference. Those others were real friends as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When your ex-husband was going to visit Kozarac, you mentioned the occasions during the time you were in Banja Luka when he visited Kozarac, did he take his automatic rifle with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what period of time you are referring to. He is not my ex-husband. He was my husband and he has remained my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Are you not divorced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it has nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So during the time that you were staying in Banja Luka between 23rd May and 27th June, you mentioned there were two occasions when your husband went to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On those occasions did he take his automatic rifle with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time he did not, but the second time he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You said that on the occasion that he went to Trnopolje with Jovo Samardzija, they went to find that man's sister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: She is married to a Muslim, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, she is not married.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: She ended up in Travnik, did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in Zenica. That is what Jovo told me afterwards, not Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why did she go to Zenica rather than stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because she was evacuated along with the rest of the Muslim population and she went in a convoy with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. When you were talking about Trnopolje, you indicated that the entire population had been evacuated to Trnopolje. First off ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That is what you said. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A part of the population from Kozarac had been evacuated to Trnopolje and the rest of them to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The part that went to Trnopolje, those were Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and a few Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that your husband had been given that automatic rifle by a man named Kusota?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is his family name. I said I did not know what his first name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why would he give that weapon to Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To take it back to the barracks in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: My question is why would he give it to Dusko Tadic and not someone else to take it back? Did he have some special relationship with Dusko Tadic or did he know that Dusko Tadic had the ability to take that back without getting in trouble?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he did not know it. He must have assumed that Dule could take it there and give it to someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: He wanted to give it away because he would get in trouble if he was caught with it, correct, since he was a deserter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because he was a deserter he was not allowed to carry arms. He just simply wanted to give it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: But, in fact, Dusko Tadic did not turn that weapon in but kept it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your apartment in Pecani that you moved into, do you know what happened to Hasan Tulundzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that before the conflict in Prijedor they left to go abroad. That is at least what I heard. He and his family left to go abroad and stay with relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You are sure that the description about the circumstances surrounding your taking over that apartment are accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You described in great detail your husband's activities and schedules while he was working with the traffic police. During that time did you work with him in the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not work with him and I did not give a detailed description. I mean, I know where he worked, but what do you mean by "detailed description"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you accompany him to his work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not accompany him to work. I simply used to come across him as he was at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time he worked in Kozarac did you work with him in the police there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you accompany him to work when he was stationed in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would visit Kozarac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You talked about one of his positions was the bridge over the Sana by the Hotel Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you go and see him there when he was assigned to that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, once I went to have my hair cut in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you then familiar with the fact that that area was one of the collection centres throughout the summer of 1992 for the Muslims and Croats who were still being rounded up and sent to the camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand what area you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The area next to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not an area from which they were being rounded up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When your husband was assigned to Kozarac you described some of his duties there. Was he also responsible for distributing aid from the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During period of 1991/1992 were there joint checkpoints in the Kozarac/Prijedor area, and by "joint" I mean guarded by both Muslims and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During 1991 there were no checkpoints. In May (sic) 1992, in the area of Kozarac there were checkpoints, where I lived only Muslim checkpoints, no joint checkpoints. I am sorry, I said in May. Checkpoints started to exist in March and April 1992. March, April, May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did some Serbs in the Kozarac area attempt to obtain weapons from the weapons storage places to distribute to the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did some Serbs in the Kozarac area plan the assignments for the Serb population that were to be put into effect if a war started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did not Dusko Tadic in fact take part in those activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there members in Kozarac of the SDS who were considered activists on behalf of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand. Please could you clear it up a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there members of the party in Kozarac, that is the SDS, who actively sought to advance the goals and policies of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our objective and the politics of the SDS were only to organise the plebiscite, that was all the duty and all our tasks. After that we had no tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What about other members of the SDS in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Approximately two weeks before the war began in the Prijedor area your husband met with the President of the SDS in Prijedor, Simo Miskovic, and the President of the opstina, Milomir Stakic, to discuss the negotiations between Kozarac officials and Prijedor officials, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband, as far as I know, was not on his own in Prijedor. He was with a group of citizens of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is it not true that prior to that meeting with the group he had a separate meeting with those two men I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your husband did not tell you about such an important meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About certain important meeting with a group of citizens from Kozarac he told me, and he went there twice on such a meeting, but I do not know that he went to any kind of a meeting on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You testified in direct about the mobilization of Dusko Tadic in mid-June 1992. When did you yourself speak -- you testified as to why he was not mobilized, excuse me, prior to that time as well -- when did you yourself speak to the Serb Ministry officials about why he had not been mobilized prior to that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On your direct testimony you explained why it was your husband had not been mobilized prior to mid-June of 1992. When did you speak with the officials regarding mobilization to determine that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not discuss anything with the authorities. My husband, that is his cousin discussed with Dule Jankovic for him to enter into the Police Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You testified that you went to Prijedor on 17 June 1992 and returned to Banja Luka on 18 June 1992. What time on the 18th did you leave Prijedor to come back -- I am sorry, what time did you leave Banja Luka to return to Prijedor? No, I am sorry, I have not ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 17th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Right. How did you travel back to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By train until Prijedor and then back to Banja Luka also by train.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That train from Prijedor to Banja Luka does not go through Kozarac, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it goes through Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So are you saying now that you went back to Banja Luka on 17th June or on 18th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I went back to Banja Luka on 18th and on 17th I arrived at Prijedor. I spent the night there and went on the following day back to Banja Luka. That is how I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With respect to the issue of Major Maric and the military police in Prijedor, were you in Prijedor when Dusko Tadic fled from the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but he did not flee on one occasion but on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you yourself receive any threats from the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from the military police but from Major Maric, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you receive those threats? Were those by letter or by phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By phone and later on also orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you know Major Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know him. I met him later on, but at that time I did not know him. We have only talked on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Finally, did Dusko Tadic tell you in June 1993 that the premises of the Local Commune and SDS in Kozarac had been robbed several times, and that the investigation into those robberies had implicated the local SDS officials themselves, including Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I know that on several occasions the office had been burgled, but that somebody robbed something, no, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: He did not tell you that the investigations had indicated that the robberies had implicated the SDS officials themselves including Dusko Tadic in those robberies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is the first time I hear it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You have mentioned a lot of dates in your testimony when you and Dusko Tadic did certain things or were in certain places. When did you begin to reconstruct these dates and events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When did you begin to reconstruct in your mind these dates and events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What events do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: All of the events that you testified to here in this courtroom where you provided dates and, in some instances, specific times for events that you and Dusko Tadic were involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some dates are concretely connected to something important and of course I remember them, and the others I sort of looked to a calendar and I found out according to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you given any materials by anyone to read in connection with your testimony in this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Have you watched any of the proceedings of this trial on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Have you ever been told not to watch the proceedings of this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Have you discussed this case with friends or relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean concretely?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Have you discussed this case, the charges involving your husband and the facts about the case, have you discussed those with friends or relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was nothing to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Have you discussed this case with other Defence witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In 1992 or 1993 was there an investigation against Dusko Tadic by the Prijedor police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there claims being made by many people that Dusko Tadic had been receiving bribes from them with respect to his duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were rumours, but nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, your Honour. Just one final question to follow up. So to your knowledge there was no official investigation in 1992 or 1993 regarding Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know. I knew about threats by the Commander of the police, but I did not know about anything officially. There were rumours that there was a case against him at the police. That is what I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did you hear those rumours from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those rumours I heard them from Dusko's brother Ljubomir Tadic and he heard about that from the brother of Dule Jankovic at the market in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One matter in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which Commander of THE police was making threats against your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule Jankovic, Dusan Jankovic, he was the Police Commander in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was he making threats against your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly which year. Since he started to work at the Local Commune in Kozarac, since then, so probably during 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What were those threats about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were not direct threats. As I was told, Ljubomir Tadic, Dule's brother, told me that Dule Jankovic is compiling a huge file about Dule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why was that? What was the file about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, Dule, when he left the police, then he had a conflict, came into conflict with the police that stayed in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What did this conflict concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the property that remained in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was his concern about the property in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he wanted that the property in Kozarac would stay there, and to revive the place so that somebody could live there in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were people wanting to take property from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By "property" what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in particular, for, example, the sawmill, the electrical mills, then the tiles on the roofs, building material, those kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who was it that was trying to take this property from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, people were taking those things under the protection of the police. That is why Dule came into conflict with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was your husband trying to do about that to stop these people connected with the police from taking the property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he wanted to prevent them doing that. He complained at the Assembly. That is why all that came about. He came into conflict with the police and with the military authorities because of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When he complained at the Assembly, was that just on one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was on several occasions, but once there was a real Municipal Assembly meeting and that is where he came into conflict with them. That was the most serious conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was this the Assembly in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who attended the Assembly meetings in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who attended the meetings. There were the municipal, the military authorities and the police, the representatives of those authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So would these have been the people who governed Prijedor at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was Dusko Tadic making allegations at these meetings that these people were protecting others who were stealing property from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know for how long he was in conflict with the authorities in Prijedor over these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the whole time up until he left Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was anyone else that you know of talking out and speaking out against these authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many were complaining. The discussion with our friends was that it was all right for Dule to have said that at the meeting, but nothing could have been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mrs. Tadic, just two questions. The first one, am I right in thinking that Vidovici is mainly a Serb or was mainly a Serb inhabited village in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That was where the polling place was for the plebiscite that was organised which you took part in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the plebiscite was not organised there. That was only written like that, but the plebescite was in an office by the church.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Because that document merely appoints your husband and you as voting officials for polling place No. 36 in Vidovici, and I wondered if that was the only polling place that you had anything to do with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, put it like this, that is the way it was written, but it was not viable to do it that way because Vidovici is far from Kozarac. So we decided for this other option up until the very last moment we did not know where would be the best place to organise it. So we decided to do it in the churchyard. There were also posters stating that the plebescite would be held in our family house, but we decided it would not be OK to do it in a private home. In Vidovici there was no official building. That is why we decided for the churchyard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So was there any voting then in your house for this plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mrs. Tadic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Tadic, you are free to leave and you are free to return home. However, you should continue to make yourself available because you may be recalled as a witness in this case. So keep in touch with Mr. Kay, and if Mr. Kay tells you that you are to report back to the Tribunal, then you should do that. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Thank you. You are excused at this time. We would like to talk with counsel just for one moment without the sound. Mrs. Tadic, you may leave. Thank you for coming. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The court adjourned until the following day).
